teaser: One flash of lightning, one tiger mid-crouch. But who exactly is surprised?
review_notes:
Félix Vallotton's 1891 review ('alpha and omega of painting') is quoted in the standard English translation.
Rousseau's later statement that the tiger is about to pounce on explorers: reported by the National Gallery.
Gap of roughly thirteen years before his next jungle picture (1904).
National Gallery acquisition in 1972 with a contribution from Walter H. Annenberg.
Mexico legend: Rousseau served in the army in France and never went to Mexico.
Direction of rain streaks (upper right to lower left) judged from the image.

lesson.text: A crack of thunder. For a split second the whole jungle turns white, and in that flash you catch a tiger in the tall grass: back arched, eyes bulging, teeth bared. Then it will be dark again. Henri Rousseau paints that split second and nothing else.

The storm is at its peak. Wind drags every branch to one side and rain comes down in sheets. Before you study the animal, check the sky. The cause of the flash is still up there, though Rousseau drew it so thin that many people walk past it.

spots.title: The bolt
spots.text: A hair-thin white line zigzags down behind the black leaves, with a second fork lower to the left. It is the lightest mark in the painting, and it sets the clock: this is happening now.

lesson.text: Now the title makes more sense. Rousseau exhibited the picture in Paris in 1891 as “Surpris!” with the exclamation mark. But who is surprised? The tiger, startled by the thunder? Or something beyond the right edge that the tiger is about to startle? French allows both readings.
Years later Rousseau settled the matter in his own way. He said the tiger was about to pounce on a group of explorers. They are nowhere on the canvas. He left the victims outside the frame.

To make you feel the weather, he tried something unusual for him. He covered the finished jungle with long slanting streaks of thin, see-through gray paint, a layer painters call a glaze. The whole scene is seen through rain.
Two forces cross in this picture.

lines.label: The rain
lines.text: The pale streaks all fall at the same slant, from upper right to lower left. Once you notice them, you find them running across leaves, trunks and sky alike.

lines.label: The wind
lines.text: The big branches bend the other way, sweeping from the trunks toward the right edge. Wind and rain pull the picture in two directions at once.

lines.label: The tiger
lines.text: His back humps up, then the body drops toward the head. He moves with the wind, to the right, toward whatever waits off the canvas.

lesson.text: This was Rousseau's first jungle. He was 47 and still a toll clerk who painted on his days off. He let people believe he had seen such forests as a soldier in Mexico. He had not. He never left France, and his tropics came from the hothouses of the Paris botanical garden.

That origin shows once you know it. The plants are a florist's mix, garden leaves and potted species blown up to the size of trees. And the tiger has the stiffness of an animal copied from a print or a stuffed specimen, not from a living cat.

lesson.title: The animal up close
lesson.text: Three details that critics of 1891 found ridiculous, and later painters found thrilling.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Round eye, ears flat, whiskers drawn one by one, a red mouth full of even teeth. It is half snarl and half fright, which is why the title works both ways.

spots.title: The tail
spots.text: Banded in black and yellow, it pokes up through the grass far to the left, like a striped snake. It shows how long the hidden body must be.

spots.title: The red tree
spots.text: One burst of scarlet leaves in a world of green and ocher. It sits exactly where the tiger is heading, a warning flare in the storm.

lesson.text: Most reviewers mocked the picture as childish. One young Swiss painter, Félix Vallotton, wrote the opposite. The tiger surprising its prey, he said, should not be missed: “it is the alpha and omega of painting.” For Rousseau, serious praise in print was a rare thing.

The praise did not lead to a jungle series, at least not right away. Rousseau waited about thirteen years before painting his next tropical forest. Nearly all of his famous jungles date from the last six years of his life.
The canvas, about 130 by 162 cm (51 by 64 in), stayed in private hands for decades. The National Gallery in London bought it in 1972.
Rousseau invented his jungle from greenhouse plants and imagination, then froze it at the exact instant of a lightning flash. The title leaves you to decide who gets the fright.

quiz.question: What moment does the painting capture?
options: A tiger sleeping after a storm
The instant of a lightning flash
quiz.explanation: A thin white bolt in the sky shows the scene is lit by lightning at that very second.

quiz.question: According to Rousseau, what is the tiger about to attack?
options: A group of explorers outside the frame
quiz.explanation: He later said the tiger was about to pounce on explorers, who are not shown.

quiz.question: How did Rousseau paint the rain?
options: He scratched the canvas with a knife
With slanting streaks of thin, see-through gray paint
quiz.explanation: He laid a glaze of transparent gray streaks over the whole scene.

quiz.question: Where did Rousseau study tropical plants?
options: In the hothouses of the Paris botanical garden
quiz.explanation: He never left France and worked from greenhouse plants in Paris.

quiz.question: Who praised the painting as “the alpha and omega of painting”?
options: The director of the National Gallery
quiz.explanation: The young Swiss painter Félix Vallotton wrote this in his 1891 review.

facts.text: This was the first jungle picture Rousseau ever painted.
facts.explanation: He painted it in 1891 and did not return to the subject for about thirteen years.

facts.text: Rousseau based the scene on his memories of military service in Mexico.
facts.explanation: He let people believe that, but he never left France.

facts.text: The explorers the tiger is hunting can be seen at the right edge.
facts.explanation: They are not on the canvas at all; Rousseau left them outside the frame.
